p.src: When at last I came to my senses, I found myself still lying flat on my back, surrounded by a great crowd of kappa. Moreover, one kappa wearing pince-nez over its thick beak was kneeling beside me with a stethoscope pressed to my chest. When that kappa saw me open my eyes, it gestured for me to keep still, then called “Quax, quax” to another kappa somewhere behind it. At once, two kappa appeared from somewhere, carrying a stretcher. They placed me on the stretcher and quietly carried me several blocks through the throng of kappa. The streets stretching along both sides of me looked no different at all from the Ginza. Shops had spread their awnings beneath rows of hairy zelkovas, while automobiles streamed along the road between the trees. Before long, the stretcher bearing me turned into a narrow side street and was carried into a house. As I learned afterward, it was the home of the kappa with the pince-nez—the home of a doctor named Chak. Chak laid me down on a neat little bed. Then he made me drink a glass of some transparent liquid medicine. I simply lay on the bed and let Chak do whatever he pleased. Indeed, every joint in my body hurt so badly that I could scarcely move at all. Chak never failed to come and examine me two or three times a day. And about once every three days, the kappa I had first encountered—a fisherman named Bag—would come to visit me as well. Kappa know far more about human beings than we human beings know about kappa. That is probably because kappa capture human beings far more often than we human beings capture kappa.

p.src: Even if “capture” is not quite the right word, human beings had often come to the land of the kappa before I did. What is more, many of them had spent the rest of their lives there. Can you guess why? Simply by virtue of being human rather than kappa, we could live without working. Indeed, according to Bag, a young road worker who had likewise arrived in this country by chance took a female kappa as his wife and lived there until his death. It must be said, however, that this female kappa was the greatest beauty in the country and also extraordinarily adept at deceiving her road-worker husband.

p.src: About a week later, under the laws of that country, I was granted the status of a “specially protected resident” and went to live next door to Chak. Though small, my house was finished with remarkable elegance. The civilization of this country, of course, did not differ greatly from that of the human world—or at least from that of Japan. A small piano stood in one corner of the sitting room overlooking the street, and framed etchings hung on the walls. The only inconvenience was that the house itself, as well as the tables and chairs, had all been made to suit the stature of kappa, so I felt as though I had been put into a child’s room. Toward dusk each day, I would welcome Chak and Bag into this room and learn the language of the kappa from them. No, they were not the only ones. Since everyone was curious about me, a specially protected resident, even Gael, the president of a glass company who went out of his way to summon Chak every day to have his blood pressure checked, would drop into this room. Yet during my first fortnight there, the one who became closest to me was still that fisherman, Bag. It was dusk on a warm, humid day. I was sitting in this room opposite Bag the fisherman, with the table between us. Then, for some reason, Bag suddenly fell silent, opened his large eyes even wider, and stared fixedly at me. Naturally, I found this strange, so I said, “Quax, Bag, quo quel, quan?” That was what I said. Translated into Japanese, this means, “Hey, Bag, what’s the matter?” But Bag did not answer.

p.src: Not only that, but he suddenly sprang to his feet, stuck out his tongue, and even made as though to leap at me like a frog. I grew more uneasy than ever, quietly rose from my chair, and was about to bolt for the doorway in a single bound. Fortunately, at that very moment, the doctor, Chack, appeared in the doorway.

p.src: “Hey, Bag—what do you think you're doing?” Still wearing his pince-nez, Chack glared at Bag as he spoke. Bag seemed thoroughly cowed; repeatedly putting a hand to his head, he apologized to Chack in these words: “I am truly, terribly sorry. The truth is, I found it amusing to see how badly I frightened this gentleman, so I got carried away and played a prank on him. Please, sir, do forgive me.”
